title_en: What Are the Telltale Signs of Low Cognition?
excerpt_en: One answer talks about highly educated people with low cognition; the other about low cognition in everyday life. Together they show something stranger than ignorance: knowledge and emotion both turned into tools of defense.
body_en:
What are the telltale signs of someone with a low level of cognition?

This question has 8,014 answers on Zhihu and more than 30 million views. Two of the most upvoted answers — one about highly educated people with low cognition, the other about low cognition in everyday life — together show that this is far more complicated than simply "being uneducated."

The first kind: highly educated, low cognition

Start with an unpopular observation: high education, low cognition.

Yale scholar Dan Kahan gave this pattern a name: identity-protective cognition. When a political belief becomes part of someone's identity, arguing against that belief feels to them like an attack on who they are, and triggers a stress response.

At that point, their knowledge, their logic, and their eloquence all switch on automatically — in service of defending the belief they already hold. You get the strange feeling that they are using polite, well-reasoned language to say something with no logic in it at all.

One person, for example, seriously argued that parliament's power to audit government finances is useless, even counterproductive. Put plainly, he had no objection at all to having no say over how his own tax money is spent — he was greatly in favor of it.

Would a normal person want a say over money they paid out of their own pocket, or would they rather have someone else decide for them? It is baffling that such common sense took hundreds of floors of argument.

More subtly, he was perfectly comfortable with the platform suppressing dissenting replies sent to him, and saw nothing wrong with it — even asking the people debating him, "Why don't you offer some useful arguments?" while ignoring the fact that nobody could post at all.

How does this psychology form? The portrait looks something like this: excellent grades from childhood, admitted to a top domestic university; abundant opportunities during the years of rapid economic growth; study abroad, then a job at a major American company; high income and respectable social status.

It is easy for such a person to tie their personal success to national development and the political system. That attribution is not entirely wrong — economic growth, education, and social stability do create opportunities. But stretching personal success into proof that the whole system is rational is survivorship bias.

More importantly, if that attribution has become part of their life story, then re-examining the system means reinterpreting decades of their own life. That price is too high.

But honestly, it is not entirely their fault. The education system can mass-produce technical elites, but it does not provide civic education. Many people solved countless math and physics problems, yet during the most critical years of character formation, they never systematically thought about questions like these: Where does the legitimacy of power come from? Why does procedural justice matter? Can the interests of the majority override the basic rights of the minority? How should you constrain a political force you support? Why protect the free expression of people you despise? How credible is a theory that cannot be falsified?

By the time their worldview hardens, changing it is difficult and painful.

The most dangerous thing about this way of thinking is that, while defending the political force they identify with, a person gradually abandons the very principles that could have protected them too.

It brings to mind Leopold Averbakh of the Soviet Union. In 1929, at just 26 years old, he was already one of the most powerful figures in Soviet literature, leading the Russian Association of Proletarian Writers and pushing for literary works to be judged by political stance. He organized campaigns against writers like Zamyatin and Pilnyak.

His crowning work came in 1934, when he co-edited "The White Sea–Baltic Canal" with Gorky and others — a book that portrayed prisoners' forced labor as a great achievement of socialist construction.

But it did not last. Just three years later, he was swept up in the Great Purge himself. On August 14, 1937, his name appeared on an execution list approved by Stalin; he was sentenced to death through a so-called "special procedure" and executed the same day, his ashes buried in the mass grave for unclaimed remains at Moscow's Donskoye Cemetery.

So be very careful when you support and enjoy one-sided free speech, because that line is not under your control. Of course you can stand outside the line and enjoy the thrill of watching dissenters fall silent. But then be ready for the day that line swallows you too.

The second kind: low cognition in everyday life

Now the everyday version. A wife asks her husband: what does low cognition look like? He lists five situations: you offer a suggestion, and he thinks you're trying to control him; you state a fact, and he thinks you're negating him; you point out a problem, and he thinks you're blaming him; you offer a solution, and he thinks you're lecturing him from above; you reason with him, and he thinks you're pressuring him with emotion.

The core is one sentence: people with low cognition want emotional validation. Go along, soothe, flatter — that feels good. Logic, judgment, and reason only annoy them.

There is an even sharper concept here, "the malice of the helped": when someone's cognitive level is not high enough, the more unreservedly you help them and treat them well, the less grateful they become — instead, a hidden hatred and contempt grows. Whoever you over-invest in, you end up carrying their fate. You keep thinking that if you are good enough, you can lift them up. In reality you cannot change them, and they only become more convinced that they are right.

Communicating with such a person is enormously draining, because you are not even on the same channel: you talk logic, they hear emotion; you talk structure, they wonder whether you look down on them. You reason, they play the feelings card; you analyze cause and effect, they ask whether you are too cold-blooded. In the end you have to give up. Trying to wake a brain with no capacity for self-reflection is futile in itself.

Their cognitive traits are easy to spot: they cannot tell facts from opinions, and judge the world through emotion and prejudice; they have no ability to tell good from bad, confuse the two, are extremely stubborn, and only believe their own choices are right; what they pursue is often objectively bad, yet they stubbornly insist it is right. You cannot get through to them, and trying to help them turns into persecuting them.

Then there is the topic-shift: you are taking apart a problem, and they question your character; you discuss a social phenomenon, and they attack your emotional intelligence; you say a phenomenon deserves reflection, and they shoot back, asking if there is something wrong with you. They never reflect on the problem itself — they only move the problem onto you.

This is no accident. It is a self-defense mechanism: unable to absorb the cognitive shock of a complex world, they can only protect their fragile sense of self by attacking the person who raised the question. Simply put: if they can't understand it, they attack you. In the end you realize you are not communicating with a person — you are fighting their defense system.

Putting it together

The two answers are really about the same thing: low cognition is not a lack of knowledge. It is knowledge and emotion both turned into tools of defense.

Educated people use logic and degrees to fortify their identity; uneducated people use emotion and attacks to protect their world. Both end up the same way: unable to hear a different opinion, and ever more certain that they are right.

To close with the second answer's conclusion: "What makes people with low cognition frightening is not how foolish they are — it is that their foolishness is self-consistent, sealed off, and aggressive."
